title: What My Grandmother Taught Me About Allah's Mercy
script: Narrator: [warmly] My grandmother lived a hard life. She lost her husband young, and she raised five children alone.
Narrator: [thoughtful] When I was small, I asked her once, were you angry at Allah for such a hard life?
Narrator: [gently] She looked at me and smiled. She said, angry? No. Allah gave me strength I did not know I had.
Narrator: [reflective] I did not understand her answer then. I was too young to understand real hardship.
Narrator: [softly] Years later, I lost my own job and struggled for many months. I remembered her words often.
Narrator: [with feeling] During that hard time, small things kept happening. A friend helped me. A stranger gave good advice. Money arrived when I needed it most.
Narrator: [warmly] I started to see these moments as more than luck. I saw them as Allah's mercy, arriving quietly, again and again.
Narrator: [thoughtful] I also started calling my grandmother more, asking her questions I never thought to ask when I was young.
Narrator: [warmly] She told me stories I had never heard, about neighbors who helped her, about small jobs that appeared just in time.
Narrator: [gently] Every story had the same pattern. Hardship, and then, quietly, help arriving from somewhere unexpected.
Narrator: [peacefully] Now I understand what my grandmother meant. Mercy does not always remove hardship completely.
Narrator: [gently] Sometimes mercy is the strength to keep walking through it, one day at a time.
Narrator: [warmly] My grandmother passed away last spring, but her words still visit me on my hardest days.
Narrator: [with feeling] I hope, one day, my own grandchildren will remember something I said the same way I remember her.
